title: YOUR HUSBAND QUOTES 1 CORINTHIANS 7 EVERY TIME YOU SAY NO TO SEX. BUT DID GOD REALLY GIVE HIM THAT RIGHT?
paragraphs: YOUR HUSBAND QUOTES 1 CORINTHIANS 7 EVERY TIME YOU SAY NO TO SEX. BUT DID GOD REALLY GIVE HIM THAT RIGHT?

When Scripture becomes pressure in the bedroom, a wife may begin to wonder whether saying no to her husband means saying no to God. But what if the very passage being used to silence her contains a truth her husband has overlooked?
She wasn't trying to reject her husband.
She was exhausted.
The children had finally fallen asleep. The dishes were still waiting in the kitchen. Her body ached from a day that seemed to demand something from her every waking minute.
All she wanted was to close her eyes.
Then she felt his hand.
"Not tonight, please. I'm really tired."
The room changed.
He pulled away. The silence became heavy.
And then came the words she had learned to dread.
"Doesn't the Bible say your body belongs to me?"
She knew what was coming.
First Corinthians. Chapter seven. Verses three through five.
He had quoted them before.
Sometimes with disappointment. Sometimes with anger. Sometimes with the confidence of a man who believed that possessing a Bible verse meant possessing the final word.
"You're supposed to fulfill your marital duty."
She stared at the ceiling.
Because now she wasn't simply dealing with a disappointed husband.
She was wrestling with something far more frightening.
Was she disappointing God?
Was her exhaustion sinful?
Was her desire to rest an act of rebellion?
Was being a good Christian wife supposed to mean surrendering her body even when her heart was hurting, her mind was overwhelmed, or she simply did not want sexual intimacy that night?
And somewhere between guilt and fear, a question began forming that she was almost afraid to ask.
If God loves me, why does obedience to Him suddenly feel like I have no voice?
Perhaps you've asked that question.
Perhaps you've never spoken it aloud.
Perhaps you love your husband deeply, believe marriage is sacred, and genuinely desire to honor the Lord.
But you have begun to dread the moment he opens his Bible during an argument about sex.
Because the Scripture that should lead both of you toward Christ has become something you fear will be used against you.
If that sounds familiar, I want you to stay with me.
Not because we're going to dismiss the Bible.
Not because we're going to pretend that marital intimacy doesn't matter.
And certainly not because we're going to replace God's design for marriage with whatever modern culture finds convenient.
We're going to do something more demanding.
We're going to read what God actually said, including the words people sometimes leave out.
And when we finish, you may discover that the same chapter your husband quotes to demand intimacy also confronts the way he treats you when you are vulnerable.
Because Scripture is not a weapon God gave husbands to win arguments against their wives.
It is the Word of God, before which husbands and wives must both bow.
And the first surprise is waiting in the original Greek.
In 1 Corinthians 7:3, the apostle Paul writes:
The King James Version translates this:
“Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband.”
Read that again.
Slowly.
The husband. Unto the wife.
Before Paul speaks about the wife's corresponding obligation, he addresses the husband.
And notice the word that follows.
ὁμοίως (homoiōs).
It means likewise, or in the same way.
Paul is establishing reciprocity.
Not a one-sided entitlement.
Not a hierarchy in which one spouse's desires automatically cancel the other's concerns.
Both spouses have responsibilities toward one another.
The Greek noun ὀφειλή (opheilē) refers to something owed, a debt or obligation. In this context, it concerns the marital obligation of sexual intimacy.
So we must be careful.
Paul really is teaching that sexual intimacy matters in marriage.
He is not describing it as an optional inconvenience that spouses may disregard without concern for one another.
Marriage includes real commitments.
Sexual neglect can wound a relationship. Persistent indifference toward a spouse's legitimate needs can become a serious marital problem.
But here is where a crucial distinction must be made.
A mutual marital obligation is not an unlimited right to another person's body on demand.
Paul does not say a husband may threaten, intimidate, punish, or force his wife into sexual activity.
He does not instruct husbands to use spiritual guilt to overcome their wives' resistance.
And he certainly does not declare that a wife's physical pain, emotional distress, illness, exhaustion, or fear must be ignored whenever her husband desires sex.
Those commands are not in the passage.
If someone wants to claim that Paul authorized coercion, that person must demonstrate it from Scripture rather than smuggling the conclusion into the text.
Now comes the verse that is frequently quoted.
First Corinthians 7:4.
“ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλ᾽ ὁ ἀνήρ, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλ᾽ ἡ γυνή.”
The King James Version reads:
“The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.”
There it is.
The verse that can make a frightened wife feel as though her body has been signed away.
But don't stop reading halfway through.
Because Paul doesn't.
He says the wife does not exercise exclusive authority over her body in marriage.
And likewise, the husband does not exercise exclusive authority over his body.
The Greek verb ἐξουσιάζει (exousiazei) comes from a word family associated with authority or the exercise of authority.
Paul deliberately applies the same principle to both spouses.
This is remarkable in its first-century setting.
In a world where women frequently possessed fewer social and legal protections than men, Paul explicitly recognizes a wife's corresponding marital claim upon her husband.
He does not present the husband as the sole sexual decision-maker.
He describes a mutual relationship.
And mutuality changes everything.
Because if a husband reads this verse and concludes, "My wife must consider my needs," he must also accept that he is commanded to consider hers.
Her body is not merely a resource for his satisfaction.
Her well-being matters.
Her experience matters.
Her dignity matters.
And a husband cannot honestly claim to be honoring Paul's teaching while disregarding the very woman Paul tells him to serve.
But we need to go deeper.
Because a dangerous misunderstanding can arise when someone hears the phrase "the husband has authority over his wife's body" and assumes that marital commitment eliminates the need for consent.
It does not.
Marriage creates a covenant of faithfulness and mutual responsibility. It does not make sexual violence righteous.
Consent is not the enemy of biblical marriage. Coercion is the enemy of the loving mutuality biblical marriage requires.
And this is where we must confront an uncomfortable reality.
Some women are not merely experiencing ordinary disagreements about sexual frequency.
They are being threatened.
Punished.
Humiliated.
Told that refusing sex makes them ungodly.
Some are pressured until they stop resisting because surrender seems easier than another argument.
Some are afraid of what their husbands might do if they refuse.
That is not the same as two spouses lovingly working through different levels of sexual desire.
And calling such pressure "biblical leadership" does not make it holy.
A husband may sincerely believe that sexual intimacy is important to his marriage.
He may feel lonely, rejected, or deeply hurt by prolonged sexual distance.
Those feelings deserve compassionate attention.
But hurt feelings do not authorize harmful behavior.
A husband's genuine need for affection does not give him permission to disregard his wife's safety or willingness.
And a wife's genuine need for rest does not mean she has abandoned her marriage.
Both realities can be acknowledged without making either spouse the enemy.
Now listen carefully to what Paul says next.
First Corinthians 7:5 begins:
“μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους, εἰ μήτι ἂν ἐκ συμφώνου πρὸς καιρόν...”
The King James Version begins:
“Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time...”
The verb ἀποστερεῖτε (apostereite) carries the idea of depriving or withholding what is due.
And the expression ἐκ συμφώνου (ek symphōnou) means by agreement or by mutual consent.
Paul is addressing intentional abstinence within marriage, especially abstinence undertaken for a season of prayer.
He warns spouses against unilaterally imposing such abstinence on each other.
That warning matters.
But so does the context.
Paul is not discussing every circumstance in which a spouse might be unable or unwilling to have sex.
He is not addressing a wife recovering from childbirth, experiencing severe pain, facing trauma, or fearing an abusive husband.
Nor does he say that a spouse must agree to sexual activity whenever the other requests it.
The passage teaches that spouses should not use sexual deprivation as a weapon. It does not teach that spouses may use Scripture to compel sexual activity.
Those are two very different things.
And confusing them can cause terrible harm.
Consider what happens when a husband says:
"If you refuse me tonight, you're disobeying God."
What has happened in that moment?
A biblical teaching about mutual marital responsibility has been turned into a threat against the wife's conscience.
Instead of inviting his wife into loving intimacy, he is using her desire to obey Christ as leverage.
And if he knows that invoking God's judgment will make her afraid to refuse, the spiritual pressure becomes especially serious.
This is often described as spiritual abuse: using religious beliefs, authority, or Scripture to control, intimidate, or harm another person.
Not every mistaken interpretation is abuse.
Not every painful conversation about sex is manipulation.
But repeated threats, intimidation, or religious pressure intended to override someone's unwillingness must not be excused simply because the person applying the pressure can quote a Bible verse.
A verse can be quoted accurately and applied sinfully.
Even Satan quoted Scripture when tempting Jesus in Matthew 4:6.
Jesus answered by honoring the fuller truth of God's Word rather than accepting a distorted application.
That should make every Christian cautious.
Because possessing the right words does not automatically mean possessing the right heart.
And this is where the husband who quotes 1 Corinthians 7 needs to open another passage.
Ephesians 5:25.
“οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.”
The King James Version says:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
The word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) is a command to love.
And Paul doesn't leave husbands to invent their own definition.
He gives them a pattern.
Jesus Christ.
Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Not by exploiting her weakness.
Not by demanding that she suffer for His personal gratification.
Not by using His authority to crush her.
But through self-giving love.
That does not mean marriage has no obligations, no difficult conversations, and no sacrifices.
It means those sacrifices must be understood through the character of Christ.
A husband cannot use 1 Corinthians 7 to demand consideration while ignoring Ephesians 5 when it demands sacrificial love from him.
And a wife should not be taught that honoring her marriage requires accepting intimidation or sexual coercion.
Husbands, this is worth asking yourself:
When your wife says she is exhausted, do you hear a person who needs your care?
Or do you hear an obstacle standing between you and something you believe you deserve?
When she says she is hurting, do you become curious about her pain?
Or angry that her pain is inconveniencing you?
When she hesitates, do you seek understanding?
Or reach for a Bible verse to end the conversation?
These questions are not meant to condemn every husband who has ever felt rejected.
They are meant to reveal something deeper.
You can be technically correct that marital intimacy matters and still be profoundly wrong in the way you pursue it.
Colossians 3:19 gives husbands another command:
“Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.”
And 1 Peter 3:7 calls husbands to live with their wives according to knowledge and to give them honor as fellow heirs of the grace of life.
Notice the pattern.
Love.
Understanding.
Honor.
Grace.
A man who wants to obey God in the bedroom cannot ignore God's commands about his behavior outside it.
And a wife who has been pressured for years may need to hear something that has rarely been said to her.
Your husband can be disappointed by your answer without being entitled to punish you for it.
You are allowed to speak honestly about your health.
You are allowed to say that something hurts.
You are allowed to express fear.
You are allowed to need rest.
You are allowed to seek medical care, counseling, or protection when necessary.
None of those realities makes you less valuable as a wife.
And none cancels your identity as a person made in the image of God.
Genesis 1:27 tells us that God created humanity in His image, male and female.
That dignity did not disappear on your wedding day.
Marriage joined your lives in covenant.
It did not erase your personhood.
And perhaps this is the part that hurts most.
Some wives desperately want to desire their husbands again.
They miss the tenderness.
The laughter.
The feeling of being wanted without being pressured.
They remember when a hand on their shoulder meant affection rather than an expectation they feared disappointing.
They remember when intimacy felt like being cherished.
Now they find themselves calculating whether refusing tonight will mean silence tomorrow.
Whether saying they're tired will lead to accusations.
Whether explaining their pain will start another argument about biblical submission.
And slowly, something beautiful begins to feel frightening.
Not because sexual intimacy is evil.
But because intimacy cannot flourish where fear is continually cultivated.
First Corinthians 13:4–5 describes love as patient and kind, not self-seeking or easily provoked.
That passage was not written exclusively about marriage, but its teaching about Christian love certainly applies within marriage.
A spouse who follows Christ should be concerned not only with receiving affection but also with whether the other person feels safe, respected, and loved.
Now imagine a different conversation.
A wife says, "I'm exhausted tonight."
Her husband feels disappointed.
He had hoped they would be close.
He misses her.
He may even feel that they have been drifting apart.
But instead of accusing her of sin, he asks:
"Are you okay?"
She tells him how overwhelmed she has been.
He listens.
Maybe they discover that the problem isn't simply sexual desire.
Maybe she is carrying an unfair share of responsibilities.
Maybe he has been feeling emotionally disconnected.
Maybe unresolved arguments have created distance.
Maybe pain during intercourse requires medical attention.
Maybe trauma needs sensitive, qualified care.
Maybe both have stopped communicating honestly.
And perhaps they need to make time for intimacy in ways that respect both spouses rather than assuming it must happen whenever one initiates it.
He doesn't pretend his feelings don't matter.
She doesn't pretend his needs don't matter.
They begin learning how to care for one another again.
That is not weakness.
That is a marriage moving toward maturity.
Because sometimes the most loving response to "not tonight" is not another argument.
It is, "Tell me what you need."
And sometimes the most loving response to a spouse who feels consistently rejected is an honest, compassionate conversation rather than indefinite silence.
The goal is not to establish one spouse as the permanent winner.
The goal is to pursue faithful, willing, loving intimacy in a covenant where both people matter.
But there is another truth we cannot avoid.
If a husband is using threats, physical force, intimidation, or persistent coercion to obtain sex, the answer is not simply to improve communication.
Safety comes first.
A person facing sexual coercion or violence should not be told to endure it quietly for the sake of maintaining a Christian marriage.
Seeking help from a trusted person, a qualified counselor, an abuse-support service, or appropriate authorities can be necessary.
If there is immediate danger, contacting emergency services or moving to a safer place may be essential.
Couples counseling is not always appropriate when one spouse is abusing or intimidating the other. Individual support from someone trained in domestic abuse may be safer.
And no pastor should use the language of forgiveness to pressure someone into remaining exposed to harm.
Forgiveness is central to Christianity.
But forgiveness is not permission for continued abuse.
Repentance is not merely saying sorry.
It involves turning away from sin.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) is commonly translated repentance, carrying the sense of a change of mind and turning toward God.
In the New Testament, genuine repentance is associated with a changed life.
That means a husband who has misused Scripture should not simply apologize for the argument and then repeat the same behavior next week.
He must confront what he has done.
He must stop using spiritual pressure.
He must respect boundaries.
He must be willing to receive correction.
And where serious harm has occurred, he must accept accountability and the consequences of his actions.
Restoring trust may take time.
Sometimes a great deal of time.
And the person harmed should not be forced to pretend healing has happened before it has.
Because reconciliation cannot be built upon the denial of truth.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than a religious slogan.
It becomes the difference between hiding sin and bringing it into the light.
Think about Jesus in John 4.
He meets a Samaritan woman whose relational history has been complicated and painful.
He knows the truth about her life.
He does not need to pretend.
But neither does He treat her as someone unworthy of being addressed with dignity.
He engages her in conversation.
He speaks truth.
He offers living water.
And she eventually becomes a witness to others about the man who told her the truth about her life.
The point is not that her circumstances are identical to those of a wife experiencing marital coercion.
They are not.
The point is that Jesus does not require people to remain hidden behind shame before they can encounter His grace.
He brings truth into the open.
And His grace calls people toward transformation.
That matters for the wife who has been silenced.
And it matters for the husband who has sinned.
Because the Gospel does not say, "Your behavior doesn't matter."
It says that sin is serious enough that Christ died for sinners, and grace is powerful enough to call sinners into a new life.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Christ did not come merely to make us feel better about ourselves.
He came to save.
To forgive.
To reconcile us to God.
To make us new.
And if a husband's understanding of biblical marriage has become an excuse for selfishness, he needs that transforming grace.
If a wife has been made to believe that God's love depends on her willingness to surrender to coercion, she needs to hear the truth of His character.
If a marriage has become a battlefield of resentment, silence, and fear, both spouses need wisdom, truth, and appropriate help.
But remember this:
Jesus does not heal a marriage by commanding its wounds to remain invisible.
He is the Savior who calls us to walk in the light.
And sometimes walking in the light begins with a trembling sentence.
"What is happening to me is not okay."
Sometimes it begins with a husband's confession.
"I have used Scripture to pressure you, and I was wrong."
Sometimes it begins with a wife saying:
"I want us to have a loving marriage, but I cannot keep living in fear."
Sometimes it begins with seeking help outside the marriage because the person causing harm refuses to listen.
And sometimes the first evidence of grace is not a dramatic reunion.
It is the end of an abusive pattern.
The beginning of accountability.
A boundary finally respected.
A person finally believed.
A home beginning to become safer.

And for couples whose struggle is not abuse but painful differences in desire, grace may look like patient conversations, medical care, renewed affection, shared responsibilities, and a commitment to understand each other without resentment.
Different marriages need different forms of help.
But no marriage needs a distorted Gospel.
The apostle Paul, who wrote 1 Corinthians 7, also wrote Philippians 2:3–4, calling believers to humility and concern for the interests of others.
That is not a command to erase your own needs.
It is a call to reject selfish ambition and consider others.
A husband should not approach marriage asking only, "What am I owed?"
A wife should not approach marriage asking only, "How can I avoid caring about my husband's needs?"
Both should ask:
"How can I honor Christ in the way I love this person?"
And where there is abuse, honoring Christ includes refusing to disguise wrongdoing as love.
Now return to that bedroom.
The exhausted wife.
The disappointed husband.
The Bible verse hanging between them.
Imagine if, instead of treating Scripture as a weapon, they allowed it to confront both of their hearts.
Imagine the husband saying:
"I want to be close to you. But I don't want you to feel forced. Can we talk about what's been happening between us?"
Imagine the wife being able to answer honestly without fearing retaliation.
Imagine them opening 1 Corinthians 7 and reading every word.
Not only the words about marital duty.
But the words about mutuality.
Not only the words about not depriving one another.
But the broader biblical commands to love, honor, show patience, and act without selfishness.
Imagine Scripture becoming a source of conviction and care rather than a tool for winning.
That does not mean every marriage will be restored.
It does not mean every harmful spouse will repent.
And it does not mean a person must remain in danger while waiting for change.
But it does mean the Word of God should never be used to conceal what God calls sin.
Perhaps you're a husband reading this, and you feel uncomfortable.
You genuinely love your wife.
You have never thought of yourself as controlling.
But you remember times when you quoted Scripture while angry.
Times when you treated her exhaustion as an insult.
Times when you made affection conditional on whether she agreed to sex.
Times when your disappointment became punishment.
If the Holy Spirit is convicting you, don't bury that conviction beneath defensiveness.
Confess what you have done.
Seek forgiveness without demanding it.
Change your behavior.
Seek qualified help if you have established patterns of coercion or intimidation.
And understand that your wife may need time, distance, and safety before trust can be rebuilt.
You do not honor Christ by insisting that your authority be recognized while refusing to take responsibility for your actions.
You honor Him by submitting your own heart to His Word.
Perhaps you're a wife reading this with tears in your eyes.
You have spent years wondering whether your discomfort made you a bad Christian.
You have prayed for God to help you become more obedient.
But no one ever explained that your husband is also accountable to Scripture.
No one told you that love does not require you to accept threats or force.
No one told you that being a faithful wife does not mean surrendering your safety.
Hear this carefully.
You are not dishonoring God by seeking protection from harm.
And if you've been pressured or forced into sexual activity, the wrongdoing committed against you is not yours to carry as guilt.
You may need time to heal.
You may need trustworthy support.
You may need to rediscover that affection can exist without fear.
God's grace does not demand that you call harm holy.
And perhaps you're a couple reading this together.
Your marriage isn't violent.
Neither of you wants to hurt the other.
But you're lonely.
One of you feels constantly rejected.
The other feels constantly pressured.
And somewhere along the way, you stopped hearing each other's hearts.
There is hope for that struggle too.
Not through guilt.
Not through scorekeeping.
Not through pretending that sexual intimacy is unimportant.
But through repentance where needed, patience, honesty, shared responsibility, and a renewed commitment to love as Christ teaches.
Because the deepest purpose of a Christian marriage is not to create two people who always get what they want.
It is to reflect covenant faithfulness shaped by the character of God.
And the character of God is not revealed through selfish domination.
It is revealed supremely in Jesus Christ.
The One who possessed all authority and yet washed His disciples' feet.
The One who confronted sin without becoming sinful.
The One who laid down His life in love.
The One who rose again so that those who trust in Him might have forgiveness and new life.
That is the Christ who must stand at the center of our understanding of marriage.
Not a Christ invented to defend our preferences.
Not a Christ quoted selectively to silence another person.
But the living Lord before whom every husband and wife is accountable.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not for the sake of an argument.
Not to embarrass anyone.
But because silence can allow painful misunderstandings to continue.
Have you ever seen Scripture used to pressure someone rather than lovingly guide them?
Have you ever struggled to distinguish marital responsibility from coercion?
Have you ever needed someone to remind you that God's Word must be read in context?
And husbands, if this has challenged you to become more patient, compassionate, and Christlike, consider commenting "Lord, teach me to love like Jesus."
Let those words be more than a public declaration.
Let them become a prayer followed by action.
Not to publicly shame a spouse.
Not to start a war between husbands and wives.
But because somewhere, a Christian woman may be carrying guilt God never intended her to carry.
And somewhere, a Christian man may be sincerely misreading a passage he has never studied carefully.
One thoughtful share could open the door to a conversation that has been avoided for years.
Because faith is not strengthened by avoiding difficult truths.
It is strengthened when we bring our questions, wounds, and assumptions beneath the authority of God's Word.
These resources are intended to help people move beyond emotional inspiration into sustained biblical learning.
Because one article may challenge your thinking.
But continued discipleship helps shape how you live.
Your salvation is a gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not something you purchase through religious contributions.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing, not pressured or compelled.

You may choose to regard that support as part of your personal charitable giving or offering, according to your convictions. It should not be presented as a required biblical tithe or a substitute for your responsibilities to your local church.
These products can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement in daily life, and opportunities to share faith with others.
But the greatest value of this community is not a discount or a product.
It is the opportunity to keep growing in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
You are still welcome here.
And God's love cannot be measured by a monthly payment.
If you believe this work is worth continuing, we would be grateful to have you help carry it forward.
And sometimes that person is the one who needs the message most.
Before you leave, return with me one final time to the woman lying awake beside her husband.
The room is quiet.
Her heart is heavy.
She has been told that Scripture requires her silence.
But now she knows something she did not know before.
God's Word is not her enemy.
The Bible does teach mutual marital responsibility.
It does call husbands and wives to care about one another's sexual needs.
But it also commands sacrificial love, patience, honor, and humility.
And it does not give anyone permission to use force, fear, or spiritual threats to obtain sex.
She may still have difficult decisions ahead.
She may need support.
Her marriage may need serious help.
Her husband may need to repent.
There may be consequences that cannot be avoided.
But she no longer has to confuse someone else's misuse of Scripture with the voice of God.
And that distinction may be the beginning of something important.
For her.
For him.
For every couple willing to exchange control for Christlike love.
For every person who has been told that faithfulness requires silence in the face of harm.
And for every believer who needs to remember that the Gospel does not excuse sin.
It exposes sin, offers forgiveness through Christ, and calls us toward a transformed life.
The cross does not teach us to use power selfishly.
It reveals the Savior who gave Himself in love.
The resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word.
And the grace of Jesus Christ calls us to become people who no longer use God's name to justify what contradicts His character.
So the next time someone quotes 1 Corinthians 7, don't be afraid to open the chapter.
Read it carefully.
Read it completely.
Read it alongside the rest of Scripture.
And ask not merely what you can demand from your spouse.
Ask what obedience to Jesus Christ requires of you.
Because a marriage is not made holy by how often someone quotes the Bible.
It is shaped toward holiness when both spouses submit to the truth of God's Word.
And sometimes the first step toward healing is discovering that the verse someone used to silence you was never permission for them to harm you.
The God whose name was used to make you afraid is not honored by your fear—He is honored when His truth is finally allowed to speak.
